paragraphs.heading: Many drawings, one molecule
paragraphs.text: Resonance, also called mesomerism, describes the bonding in certain molecules or polyatomic ions by combining several contributing structures into one resonance hybrid. It belongs to valence bond theory and is used when no single Lewis structure can capture the bonding. It is especially valuable when electrons are delocalized. The hybrid is the accurate structure, an average of the contributing structures, which are only hypothetical.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is needed
paragraphs.text: For many substances, one Lewis structure, with atoms obeying the octet rule and bonds of whole-number order, explains measured features such as bond lengths, angles and dipole moment. Sometimes, though, more than one structure can be drawn, and the measurements fit none of them. Chemists then treat several contributing structures together as an average and call the result a resonance hybrid.

paragraphs.heading: The nitrite example
paragraphs.text: In the nitrite ion, NO₂^(–), both N–O bonds have the same length, yet no single Lewis structure gives them the same bond order. Both measure 125 pm, between a typical N–O single bond at 145 pm and an N–O double bond at 115 pm. Averaging the two contributing structures makes each bond halfway between single and double, a bond order of 1.5. That squares the drawing with the measured fact that the two bonds are equivalent.

paragraphs.heading: Lower energy
paragraphs.text: Spreading electrons out lowers the potential energy of a system, so any species described by a resonance hybrid is steadier than each of its contributing structures. With the electrons spread more evenly over the molecule, they repel each other less. The energy gap between the real species and the lowest-energy contributing structure is called the resonance energy or delocalization energy. Its size depends on the assumptions and methods used, and it is not a quantity that can be measured.

paragraphs.heading: Not flipping back and forth
paragraphs.text: Resonance is different from isomerism. Isomers share a formula but are distinct substances with their atoms arranged differently in space, while resonance contributors differ only in how electrons are assigned to atoms on paper. A hybrid does not mean electrons shift back and forth between positions; it is one structure with a single well-defined geometry and electron distribution. A narwhal makes a good comparison: it can be described as part unicorn, with one horn, and part leviathan, a large whale-like creature. It never switches between the two, and neither of them exists outside the imagination, yet the description still fits it well.

paragraphs.heading: How it is drawn
paragraphs.text: Contributing structures are usually separated by double-headed arrows (↔), which should not be confused with the equilibrium arrow (⇌). The whole set may be enclosed in large square brackets to show it pictures one molecule or ion. In a hybrid structure, pi bonds taking part in resonance are drawn as curves or dashed lines. In benzene and other aromatic rings, a solid circle is sometimes drawn to show the delocalized pi electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Benzene's puzzle
paragraphs.text: The idea was first put forward in 1899, in the Partial Valence Hypothesis of Johannes Thiele. It was meant to explain why benzene was more stable than August Kekulé's 1865 structure, with alternating single and double bonds, would lead one to expect. Thiele proposed that each carbon-carbon bond in benzene sits between a single and a double bond. This also explained isomer counts: Kekulé's structure predicts four dibromobenzene isomers, but in reality there are three, and only one of them is ortho.
